trip_options.title: Budget Explorer - Lisbon, Portugal
trip_options.description: Save money without sacrificing the experience. Perfect for travelers who value authentic local experiences over luxury.

experiences.name: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour

day_by_day.morning: No activities scheduled — flight arrives at 13:00. Use this time to rest on the plane and prepare your Lisbon plans.
day_by_day.afternoon: Arrive at Lisbon Humberto Delgado Airport at 13:00. Take the Metro (Linha Vermelha/Red Line) to the city center for around €1.50 using a reloadable Viva Viagem card — the most budget-friendly airport transfer. Check in to Lisbon City Stay, freshen up, then take a gentle orientation stroll through the Baixa (Downtown) district. Explore Praça do Comércio, the grand riverside square, and walk along the Tagus waterfront — both completely free.
day_by_day.evening: Head up to the Alfama district for your first taste of authentic Lisbon. Wander the narrow cobblestone streets and find a miradouro (viewpoint) such as Portas do Sol to watch the sunset over the city rooftops for free. Then settle in for dinner at a local tasca (traditional tavern).

meals.breakfast: Eat on the plane or grab a quick pastel de nata (custard tart, ~€1.20) and a bica (espresso, ~€0.80) at a local café near the airport or hotel upon arrival.
meals.lunch: Grab a quick prato do dia (dish of the day) at a local workers' café in Baixa — typically €7–9 including bread, drink, and dessert.
meals.dinner: Tasca do Chico or a similar neighborhood tasca in Alfama — try bacalhau à brás (codfish) or grilled sardines for €10–13. Look for a menu turístico (tourist menu) for best value.

day_by_day.notes: Purchase a 24-hour or rechargeable Viva Viagem Metro card at the airport (€0.50 card fee + credit). Wear comfortable walking shoes — Lisbon is famously hilly. Keep euros in small denominations for cafés and tascas.

day_by_day.morning: Start the day with a classic Lisbon breakfast at a local pastelaria near the hotel. Then visit the Castelo de São Jorge (St. George's Castle), one of Lisbon's most iconic historical landmarks perched above the city. Admission is €15 (standard) — check for discounts or visit the free exterior terraces and surrounding Mouraria neighborhood to save money. Explore the medieval walls and enjoy panoramic views of the city and Tagus River.
day_by_day.afternoon: Descend into the Alfama district, Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood. Visit the free exterior of the Sé de Lisboa (Lisbon Cathedral, free entry to the nave), then wander through the labyrinthine streets. Stop at Feira da Ladra, Lisbon's famous flea market held on Tuesdays and Saturdays at Campo de Santa Clara — perfect for browsing vintage finds and local crafts at no cost.
day_by_day.evening: Experience a free or low-cost Fado moment — many bars in Alfama offer fado vadio (amateur fado) in the evenings with just the cost of a drink (€2–4). Alternatively, sit at an outdoor café in Largo do Intendente and soak up the local atmosphere.

meals.breakfast: Pastelaria in Baixa or Alfama — pastel de nata + coffee for ~€2–3.
meals.lunch: Pick up a bifana (pork sandwich, ~€2.50–3.50) or a prego (beef sandwich) from a street stall or traditional café near Alfama — a true Lisbon street food staple.
meals.dinner: A Cevicheria or budget alternative: try Solar dos Presuntos or a local cervejaria (beer hall) near Intendente for a hearty Portuguese meal — budget €12–15 per person including a glass of house wine.

day_by_day.notes: Saturday is flea market day at Feira da Ladra — arrive by 9–10am for the best browsing. The Alfama streets are steep; take your time and bring water. Many churches offer free entry to their main nave but charge for cloisters or museums.

day_by_day.morning: Take Tram 28E (iconic yellow tram, €3 with Viva Viagem card) from Martim Moniz through Alfama and Estrela — a scenic and budget-friendly ride through Lisbon's historic neighborhoods. Alight at the Basílica da Estrela (free entry) and admire its stunning baroque interior. Stroll through the adjacent Jardim da Estrela, a beautiful public garden perfect for a relaxed Sunday morning picnic.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour experience — spend a culinary afternoon at this iconic food hall in Cais do Sodré. Sample the best of Portuguese cuisine from award-winning chefs and local vendors. Budget €15–25 for a satisfying spread of small plates including items like grilled octopus, bacalhau croquettes, and a glass of vinho verde. This is an ideal introduction to the breadth of Portuguese gastronomy in one place.
day_by_day.evening: Walk along the LX Factory, a hip creative hub in a repurposed industrial complex (free to enter, open Sundays with a market). Browse artisan stalls, street art, and independent shops. Enjoy a casual dinner at one of the more affordable restaurants inside the complex.

meals.breakfast: Pick up fresh bread rolls and local cheese from a Sunday morning mini-mercado (small grocery) and enjoy a picnic breakfast in Jardim da Estrela — ~€3–4.
meals.lunch: Time Out Market — budget €15–20 for a satisfying mix of Portuguese small plates and a drink.
meals.dinner: LX Factory restaurants or a nearby tasca in Alcântara — look for a prato do dia or grilled fish option for €10–14.

day_by_day.notes: Sunday LX Factory market runs roughly 10am–7pm and is very popular — visit in the afternoon after Time Out Market. Tram 28E can get crowded on weekends; watch your belongings. Time Out Market is busiest at lunch — arriving slightly before or after peak hours (1–2pm) helps.

day_by_day.morning: Take the train from Cais do Sodré station to Belém (€1.50 each way, ~10 minutes) for a full morning of UNESCO World Heritage history. Visit the Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking masterpiece of Manueline architecture — admission is €10 (or free on the first Sunday of the month). Explore the ornate cloisters and the church where Vasco da Gama is buried.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue the Belém Historical Landmarks experience. Walk to the iconic Torre de Belém (Tower of Belém) along the riverside promenade — admission is €6. Also visit the nearby Padrão dos Descobrimentos (Monument to the Discoveries, exterior free) and enjoy the sweeping views of the Tagus. Stop at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery (since 1837) for the world-famous custard tarts — just €1.30 each, eaten warm with cinnamon and powdered sugar. This is a non-negotiable Lisbon experience.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon via train. Spend the evening exploring the Chiado and Bairro Alto neighborhoods — browse independent bookshops like Livraria Bertrand (the world's oldest operating bookshop, free to browse), and enjoy the lively street atmosphere as Bairro Alto comes alive at night.

meals.breakfast: Café near Cais do Sodré station before catching the train — coffee and toast (torrada) for ~€2.50.
meals.lunch: Pastéis de Belém for the famous tarts (€1.30 each, get 2–3!) plus a light snack, or find a café near the monastery for a prato do dia (~€8–10).
meals.dinner: Bairro Alto — try Zé da Mouraria or a similar local tasca for a hearty Portuguese dinner with wine for €12–15. The neighborhood has many affordable, authentic options away from tourist traps.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is about 6km west of central Lisbon — the Cais do Sodré train is the cheapest and fastest option (avoid taxis). The Jerónimos Monastery and Torre de Belém are close to each other but involve some walking along the riverside. Bring sunscreen as the Belém waterfront is very exposed.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the Mouraria neighborhood, the historic heart of Lisbon's Moorish heritage and one of the city's most authentic and multicultural areas. Visit the free Museu do Fado (exterior and surrounding streets) and the beautiful Intendente square. Climb to the free Miradouro da Graça for arguably the best panoramic view in all of Lisbon — less touristy than other viewpoints and completely free.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Museu Nacional do Azulejo (National Tile Museum) — admission is €5 and it's one of Lisbon's most unique and rewarding museums, showcasing the history of the iconic Portuguese azulejo (decorative tile) from the 15th century to today. The museum is housed in a stunning former convent. Afterward, head back toward the city center for last-minute souvenir shopping at Mercado de Campo de Ourique or local shops in Chiado — look for affordable Portuguese products like tinned fish (conservas), ginjinha (cherry liqueur), and cork items.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner in the Bica or Cais do Sodré area. Enjoy a final leisurely Portuguese meal and a glass of local wine. Take a last evening stroll along the Ribeira waterfront, watching the lights reflect on the Tagus River.

meals.breakfast: Final Lisbon breakfast at a neighborhood pastelaria — galão (milky coffee) and a croissant or pastel de nata for ~€2.50.
meals.lunch: Mercado de Campo de Ourique food market — a local alternative to Time Out Market with authentic stalls and lower prices. Budget €8–12 for a full meal.
meals.dinner: Cervejaria Ramiro (splurge option, ~€25–30) or a more budget-friendly final dinner at a local tasca near the hotel — try caldo verde (green soup), grilled fish, and a glass of house wine for €13–16. Toast to a wonderful trip!

day_by_day.notes: Tuesday is Feira da Ladra flea market day again if you missed Saturday's edition. The Museu do Azulejo is slightly east of the center — take Bus 718 or 742 from Praça do Comércio (~€1.50). Pack any purchased conservas (tinned fish) in your checked luggage as they may trigger airport security in hand luggage. Keep your Viva Viagem Metro card topped up for any remaining travel.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) to central Lisbon and check in to Lisbon City Stay. Freshen up and get oriented with a leisurely stroll around your neighborhood.
day_by_day.afternoon: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour: Head to the iconic Time Out Market in Cais do Sodré (easily reachable by tram or a short taxi ride). Spend the afternoon sampling the best of Portuguese cuisine — try bifanas, bacalhau croquettes, pastéis de nata, and local wines. A perfect, low-effort introduction to Lisbon's food scene after a long journey.
day_by_day.evening: Wander along the Ribeira waterfront promenade at sunset. Enjoy the views over the Tagus River, then settle into a traditional tasca (taverna) nearby for a relaxed dinner.

meals.breakfast: Skip or grab a quick coffee and pastel de nata at the airport or a café near the hotel upon arrival.
meals.lunch: Time Out Market — budget €15–20 per person grazing across multiple stalls for a varied Portuguese spread.
meals.dinner: Taberna da Rua das Flores or similar traditional tasca in Chiado/Bairro Alto — expect €25–35 per person for petiscos (Portuguese tapas) and a glass of wine.

day_by_day.notes: Keep Day 1 light and flexible to recover from travel. The Time Out Market is open until midnight, so timing is very flexible. Validate your transport card (Viva Viagem) at the airport for easy metro and tram use all week.

day_by_day.morning: Alfama District Walking Tour: Start your morning with a guided walking tour through Alfama, Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighborhood. Explore narrow medieval alleyways, Moorish-era architecture, and hidden miradouros (viewpoints). Visit the Miradouro da Graça for sweeping panoramic views over the city and the Tagus.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue exploring Alfama independently — visit the Sé de Lisboa (Lisbon Cathedral), one of the city's oldest churches, with a modest entry fee. Browse the local Sunday antiques and flea market at Feira da Ladra (Thieves' Market) at Campo de Santa Clara if it's running. Absorb the authentic neighborhood atmosphere.
day_by_day.evening: Alfama Fado Show: Return to Alfama for an intimate Fado performance at a traditional casa de fado such as Parreirinha de Alfama or Mesa de Frades. Most shows begin around 20:00–21:00 and include dinner. Experience Portugal's most soulful musical tradition in its historic birthplace.

meals.breakfast: Café near the hotel — coffee and a pastel de nata or tosta mista (toasted sandwich), €3–5.
meals.lunch: A Cevicheria or a local restaurant in Alfama — try arroz de marisco (seafood rice) or grilled sardines, €15–20 per person.
meals.dinner: Included or paired with the Fado show dinner — budget €35–45 per person including the music cover charge, food, and house wine at a mid-range casa de fado.

day_by_day.notes: Book the Fado show in advance, especially for a Sunday evening — popular venues fill up quickly. Wear comfortable walking shoes as Alfama's cobblestone streets are steep and uneven. The guided walking tour typically runs 2–3 hours.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical Landmarks: Take Tram 15E or the train from Cais do Sodré westward to Belém. Begin the morning at the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking example of Manueline architecture built in the 16th century. Explore the ornate cloisters and the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões. Entry is €10 per person.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue in Belém with a visit to the iconic Tower of Belém (Torre de Belém), standing sentinel at the edge of the Tagus River. Afterward, make the essential pilgrimage to Pastéis de Belém — the original home of the pastel de nata since 1837. Enjoy the custard tarts warm from the oven, dusted with cinnamon and powdered sugar, right at the source. Also consider a quick stop at the Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos).
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the elegant Chiado neighborhood. Visit the historic Livraria Bertrand (world's oldest operating bookshop) and browse boutique shops. Enjoy a relaxed dinner in Chiado or neighboring Bairro Alto.

meals.breakfast: Full Portuguese breakfast at a local café near the hotel — coffee, fresh orange juice, toast with butter and jam, €5–8.
meals.lunch: Pastéis de Belém for the iconic tarts (€1.50 each), plus a light lunch at a nearby café in Belém — €12–18 per person.
meals.dinner: Tasca do Chico or Taberna da Rua das Flores in Chiado — traditional Portuguese petiscos and main courses, €25–35 per person with wine.

day_by_day.notes: Arrive at Jerónimos Monastery early (opens 10:00) to beat the crowds. The Tower of Belém can have queues — consider booking tickets online in advance. Belém is approximately 6–7 km west of central Lisbon; Tram 15E is scenic but slow; the train from Cais do Sodré is faster.

day_by_day.morning: National Azulejo Museum & Tile Workshop: Visit the Museu Nacional do Azulejo, housed in a magnificent 16th-century convent in the Xabregas neighborhood (reachable by Bus 794 or Uber). Explore five centuries of Portuguese decorative tile art, including the remarkable 36-meter panoramic azulejo panel depicting pre-earthquake Lisbon. Participate in a hands-on tile painting workshop if available (book ahead, ~€20–30 extra).
day_by_day.afternoon: Mouraria & Intendente Neighborhood Food & History Walk: Make your way to Mouraria, Lisbon's historic Moorish quarter and multicultural heart. Follow a self-guided or organized food and history walk through this vibrant, authentic neighborhood. Discover hidden squares, street art, diverse food stalls, and the Intendente neighborhood's recent revival. Visit the Largo do Intendente plaza and its eclectic mix of old and new Lisbon.
day_by_day.evening: Enjoy the lively atmosphere of Mouraria or nearby Martim Moniz square, which buzzes with multicultural food stalls and street life in the evenings. Have dinner at a local restaurant in the area, sampling cuisine that reflects Lisbon's diverse immigrant community.

meals.breakfast: Coffee and pastry at a local pastelaria near the hotel — €4–6.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at the Azulejo Museum café or a nearby restaurant in Xabregas — €12–18 per person.
meals.dinner: Restaurant in Mouraria/Intendente area — try traditional Portuguese or fusion dishes reflecting the neighborhood's multicultural character, €20–30 per person.

day_by_day.notes: The Azulejo Museum is closed on Mondays, so Tuesday is ideal. The museum is a hidden gem and less crowded than major sites — allow 2–3 hours. Mouraria is best explored on foot; the neighborhood is hilly but very walkable. Keep valuables secure in busy market areas.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the Príncipe Real neighborhood, one of Lisbon's most charming and upscale residential areas. Visit the weekend organic market at Jardim do Príncipe Real (check if running), browse antique shops and independent boutiques, and enjoy the shaded garden square. Stop at the fascinating underground Reservatório da Mãe d'Água cistern and the nearby Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) for a dose of Portuguese painting, sculpture, and decorative arts.
day_by_day.afternoon: Final afternoon of leisure and souvenir shopping. Head to the Baixa-Chiado area for last-minute Portuguese gifts — pick up quality conservas (tinned fish), local wines, ginjinha (cherry liqueur), or azulejo-inspired ceramics. Revisit any favorite spots or neighborhoods. Consider one last viewpoint visit — Miradouro de Santa Catarina (Adamastor) for a final sweeping view of the Tagus and the 25 de Abril Bridge.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a special restaurant to celebrate the trip. Treat yourself to a slightly elevated dining experience at a well-regarded Portuguese restaurant such as Cervejaria Ramiro (famous for seafood) or Solar dos Presuntos for classic Portuguese cuisine — a memorable final meal in Lisbon.

meals.breakfast: Brunch at a café in Príncipe Real — try a full Portuguese brunch spread with eggs, cheese, charcuterie, and fresh juice, €10–15.
meals.lunch: Light snack or petiscos at a wine bar in Chiado during shopping — €10–15 per person.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a quality mid-range to slightly upscale restaurant — budget €40–55 per person for a full seafood or traditional Portuguese meal with wine.

day_by_day.notes: If your departure flight is on May 20 or later, keep the evening relaxed. Pack the night before to avoid morning stress. Lisbon Airport is well connected — Metro (Red Line) takes about 20–25 minutes from central Lisbon. Allow extra time for security on busy travel days. Consider purchasing a bottle of local wine or ginjinha as a final souvenir.

End the night with an intimate, authentic Fado performance at a premium Fado house such as Clube de Fado or Sr. Fado.

meals.breakfast: Not applicable (in-flight or at airport upon arrival)
meals.lunch: Upon arrival, enjoy a welcome lunch at the hotel restaurant or nearby Bairro do Avillez by chef José Avillez — a refined Portuguese bistro offering elevated traditional cuisine in the heart of Chiado.
meals.dinner: Dinner included as part of the Fado show experience at a premium Fado restaurant in Alfama, featuring a curated menu of traditional Portuguese dishes paired with fine Alentejo wines.

day_by_day.notes: Arrange a private airport transfer in advance through the hotel concierge. Confirm the Fado show reservation prior to travel — premium Fado houses require advance booking. Dress smart-casual for the evening.

Explore five centuries of Portuguese decorative tile art and participate in a private hands-on azulejo tile-painting workshop to create your own souvenir.
day_by_day.afternoon: Mouraria & Intendente Neighborhood Food & History Walk — Discover Lisbon's multicultural soul in Mouraria, the ancient Moorish quarter. Join a premium guided food and history walk through vibrant streets, tasting traditional petiscos (Portuguese tapas), local cheeses, cured meats, and regional wines at curated stops. Visit the historic Intendente square and hear stories of the neighborhood's rich layered heritage.
day_by_day.evening: Enjoy a relaxed evening in the Príncipe Real neighborhood, one of Lisbon's most sophisticated districts. Browse the antique market and upscale design shops before dinner.

meals.breakfast: Lavish breakfast at the hotel — freshly baked pastéis de nata, smoked ham, local cheeses, fresh fruit, and specialty Portuguese coffee.
meals.lunch: Included within the Mouraria Food & History Walk — curated tastings at local specialty spots including traditional tascas and artisan producers.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Alma, a Michelin-starred restaurant by chef Henrique Sá Pessoa, offering a sophisticated contemporary Portuguese tasting menu with exceptional wine pairings.

day_by_day.notes: Book the private tile workshop session at the Azulejo Museum in advance as slots are limited. Wear comfortable walking shoes for the Mouraria neighborhood walk. Alma restaurant requires reservations well in advance.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical Landmarks — Take a private chauffeured car to the Belém district. Begin with a guided visit to the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a masterpiece of Manueline architecture. Admire the ornate cloisters and the tomb of explorer Vasco da Gama. Continue to the iconic Tower of Belém on the Tagus riverbank, exploring its history as a symbol of Portugal's Age of Discovery.
day_by_day.afternoon: Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour — Head to the legendary Time Out Market in Cais do Sodré for a premium culinary afternoon. Sample the best of Portuguese cuisine from award-winning chefs and artisan producers — from grilled seafood and bacalhau (salt cod) dishes to gourmet cheeses, charcuterie, and traditional sweets. Pair tastings with local craft beers and fine wines.
day_by_day.evening: Sunset cocktails at a rooftop bar with panoramic views over the Tagus River and city skyline — Hotel Bairro Alto rooftop or Park Bar Lisbon are excellent choices. Follow with a relaxed dinner in the Cais do Sodré waterfront area.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel, followed by the iconic Pastéis de Belém experience — freshly baked custard tarts at the original Pastéis de Belém bakery (founded 1837), just steps from the monastery.
meals.lunch: Gourmet tastings at Time Out Market — curated selections from top vendors including chef Henrique Sá Pessoa's counter and premium seafood stations.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Pesca, a refined seafood restaurant in Príncipe Real, specializing in sustainable Portuguese fish and shellfish with an outstanding natural wine list.

day_by_day.notes: Arrive at Jerónimos Monastery early to avoid Sunday crowds. Pre-book skip-the-line tickets for both Belém monuments. The private car to Belém takes approximately 20 minutes from central Lisbon. Pastéis de Belém can have queues — arrive before 9:30 AM if possible.

day_by_day.morning: Private guided tour of the Palácio Nacional de Sintra or Palácio da Pena in nearby Sintra (45-minute drive from Lisbon). Explore the fairytale Romanticist palace perched dramatically atop a forested hill, with stunning panoramic views of the Atlantic coastline and surrounding Serra de Sintra. Wander the lush palace gardens.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to Lisbon and explore the São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) — a Moorish hilltop fortress overlooking the entire city and the Tagus River. Enjoy a private guided tour of the castle's history spanning Phoenician, Roman, Moorish, and Portuguese eras. Afterward, wander through the charming streets of Alfama at a leisurely pace.
day_by_day.evening: Experience Lisbon's vibrant nightlife scene with a premium wine tasting experience at a sophisticated wine bar such as By the Wine (José Maria da Fonseca) in Chiado, featuring rare Dão, Douro, and Alentejo varietals guided by a sommelier.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel before departing for Sintra.
meals.lunch: Lunch in Sintra village at Tascantiga or Incomum by Luis Santos — a refined restaurant offering contemporary takes on traditional Sintra regional cuisine including travesseiros (almond pastries) and queijadas.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Belcanto, José Avillez's two-Michelin-starred flagship restaurant in Chiado — one of Portugal's most celebrated fine dining experiences, offering a creative tasting menu rooted in Portuguese culinary heritage with exceptional wine pairings. Reservations are essential and should be booked months in advance.

day_by_day.notes: Arrange a private driver for the Sintra excursion. Book Palácio da Pena tickets online in advance. Belcanto reservations are extremely sought after — secure your table as early as possible, ideally when planning the trip.

day_by_day.morning: Spend a leisurely final morning exploring the upscale Príncipe Real neighborhood — visit the Jardim do Príncipe Real garden, browse the renowned antique and design market, and stop into specialty food shops such as A Cevicheria or Comida Independente for gourmet Portuguese products to bring home as gifts.
day_by_day.afternoon: Visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) — Portugal's most important art museum, housing masterpieces of Portuguese and European art, including the stunning Panels of São Vicente de Fora polyptych. Enjoy a private guided tour of the museum's highlights. Afterward, take a final scenic tram ride on the historic Tram 28 through Lisbon's hilly neighborhoods for a nostalgic farewell to the city.
day_by_day.evening: Farewell dinner at a premium restaurant with river views — Varanda Restaurant at Four Seasons Hotel Ritz Lisbon or Panorâmico de Lisboa offer spectacular panoramic settings. Toast to an unforgettable Lisbon experience with a glass of vintage Port wine.

meals.breakfast: Final indulgent breakfast at the hotel — order à la carte from the full premium menu including smoked salmon, eggs Benedict, artisan breads, and fresh-squeezed orange juice.
meals.lunch: Light gourmet lunch at A Cevicheria in Príncipe Real, known for its creative Portuguese-inspired seafood dishes and vibrant atmosphere.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at Varanda Restaurant (Four Seasons Ritz Lisbon) — elegant contemporary Portuguese cuisine with impeccable service, panoramic city views, and an extensive cellar of Portugal's finest wines. Conclude with a glass of 20-year Tawny Port.

day_by_day.notes: Allow time for last-minute souvenir shopping — premium options include handcrafted azulejo tiles, aged Port wine, artisan cork products, and Portuguese linen. Confirm departure transfer with the hotel concierge. If departing on May 20, ensure check-out is arranged and luggage storage is available for a late departure.
